sections.title: Chapter 11 as a reset button
ps: Chapter 11 lets a company keep operating while restructuring debt: creditors trade their loans for new equity, old shareholders get diluted or wiped, and the business emerges with a lighter balance sheet

Emergence packages often include warrants for the old stakeholders — rights to buy shares at set strikes — as a lottery ticket on recovery; a penny-strike warrant is essentially free stock if the company survives
Those warrants live on as accounting time bombs: as liabilities re-measured every quarter, they make reported earnings swing by hundreds of millions in whichever direction the stock moved

The deeper lesson: capital-intensive commodity businesses (like bitcoin mining) carry existential cycle risk; the same sites and grid connections, re-let to AI tenants on take-or-pay contracts, become defensible infrastructure

sections.title: The four-stage power funnel
ps: Gross utility power: what the grid contracts allow the site to draw — the press-release number
Leasable power: the portion that can be sold to customers as IT load after cooling/overhead — typically ~2/3 of gross
Leased power: committed under signed contracts — the backlog number

Billable power: service commenced and generating invoices — the only stage that is revenue. Tracking a landlord means tracking how fast MW move down this funnel, and 'ahead of schedule' at the last stage is the strongest execution signal there is

sections.title: Anatomy of a take-or-pay colocation contract
ps: A monthly base license fee per MW with an annual escalator (~2.5-3%), paid whether or not the tenant uses the capacity, for 12-15 years with renewal options

Customer-funded fit-out: the tenant advances $1-1.5M/MW toward construction, booked as deferred revenue and credited back against a capped share of monthly fees — the tenant co-finances its own building
Power costs pass through at no markup; the landlord's margin (~60% at segment level, 80%+ per contract) lives entirely in the license fee
Compare contracts in $ per MW-year (total value ÷ MW ÷ years): it's the rent-per-square-foot of AI infrastructure, and reveals which tenant pays more for the same megawatt

sections.title: When shareholders say no: M&A lessons
ps: An all-stock deal at a fixed exchange ratio with no collar transfers all the acquirer's share-price volatility to the target's holders — if the acquirer's stock falls 40% before closing, so does the deal value
Proxy advisors (ISS, Glass Lewis) can sink a merger: their recommendations swing index-fund votes, which often decide close contests
A single-bidder process with no market check is the recurring governance sin — without competing bids, there's no evidence the price is right

The 'merger cap': while a stock deal is pending, the target trades tethered to the offer — if peers re-rate upward during the pendency, the deal literally caps shareholders out of the sector rally, which is exactly the argument that kills it

sections.title: Reading GAAP when warrants and pivots pollute it
ps: Warrant mark-to-market: stock up → liability up → GAAP loss; stock down → GAAP gain. The sign of net income can be exactly backwards as a business signal

Conversion impairments: demolishing mining halls for AI requires writing the old assets off when the demolition is committed — keeping them capitalized overstates assets, and getting this wrong can force a restatement (non-reliance on past filings, amended 10-K/Qs, and a credibility discount)
Adjusted figures diverge by provider: different data services make different calls on excluding warrant swings and impairments, so the same quarter can be a 'beat' at one and a 'miss' at another
Anchor lines to watch instead: segment revenue and gross margin, billable MW, cash and liquidity, and the contracted backlog — the four that can't be flattered by fair-value accounting

sections.title: Chip vendors as tenants: the second-source dynamic
ps: GPU vendors now compete through infrastructure: locking up hosting capacity for their silicon guarantees their customers somewhere to run it — a hosting channel as a competitive weapon

A challenger vendor (to the dominant GPU maker) pays up for capacity because the alternative is its chips having no home — which is why a second-anchor deal can price 20%+ richer per MW-year than the first
Equity warrants for the tenant recur across the sector (Google at TeraWulf, AMD here, NVIDIA at IREN/Nebius): the tenant/backstopper takes upside in the landlord as part of the price of commitment
Two 500 MW-class anchors from different ecosystems is the diversification target the whole cohort chases — one tenant is a dependency; two is a market

flashcards.q: What does Chapter 11 actually do for an over-levered infrastructure company?
flashcards.a: It keeps the business operating while creditors swap debt for new equity. The company emerges with a lighter balance sheet and new ownership — the assets and grid connections survive intact even as the old shareholders are diluted or wiped.

flashcards.q: Why do bankruptcy-emergence warrants haunt earnings for years?
flashcards.a: They're liabilities re-measured each quarter at fair value. When the stock rises the liability grows and GAAP books a loss (and vice versa) — so reported net income moves opposite to business success, by hundreds of millions.

flashcards.q: Order the four stages of the power funnel and name the only one that's revenue.
flashcards.a: Gross utility power → leasable → leased → billable. Only billable MW (service commenced, invoicing) is revenue; everything upstream is potential.

flashcards.q: How does customer-funded fit-out work in a colocation lease?
flashcards.a: The tenant advances ~$1-1.5M/MW toward construction; the landlord books it as deferred revenue and credits it back against a capped share of monthly fees. The tenant co-finances its own building, cutting the landlord's capex at the cost of near-term cash billing.

flashcards.q: What single metric compares two colocation contracts fairly?
flashcards.a: Dollars per MW-year: total contract value ÷ MW ÷ years. It's the rent-per-square-foot of AI infrastructure — and reveals when a newer tenant is paying 20%+ more for the same megawatt.

flashcards.q: Why is a no-collar, all-stock merger dangerous for the target's shareholders?
flashcards.a: The fixed exchange ratio passes every move in the acquirer's stock straight through to the deal value. If the acquirer's shares slide 40% before closing, so does the price — with no floor and no cash election.

While a stock deal is pending, the target trades tethered to the implied offer. If sector peers re-rate upward during the pendency, the deal caps shareholders out of the rally — a core activist argument for voting no.

flashcards.q: Who are ISS and Glass Lewis and why can they decide a merger vote?
flashcards.a: The two dominant proxy-advisory firms. Index funds and many institutions follow their voting recommendations, so an AGAINST from both can swing the decisive votes in a close contest.

flashcards.q: Why does converting a mining hall to AI hosting create restatement risk?
flashcards.a: Once demolition of the old assets is committed, accounting requires impairing them; keeping them capitalized overstates assets. Getting the timing wrong across multiple quarters can force non-reliance on past filings and amended reports.

flashcards.q: The same quarter shows a +1,000% EPS beat at one data service and a huge miss at another. How?
flashcards.a: Different adjusted-EPS conventions: one excludes warrant fair-value swings and impairments, the other doesn't. On warrant-heavy quarters the same GAAP number produces opposite verdicts — read segment revenue and billable MW instead.

flashcards.q: Why would a challenger chip vendor lease half a gigawatt of hosting capacity?
flashcards.a: Silicon without somewhere to run is unsellable. Locking hosting capacity guarantees its customers deployment homes — a hosting channel as a weapon against the dominant vendor's neocloud ecosystem — and it pays a premium for it.

flashcards.q: Why is a second 500 MW-class anchor tenant transformative for a landlord?
flashcards.a: One anchor is a dependency — its credit and execution are effectively your P&L. A second anchor from a different ecosystem turns the asset base into a market, improves pricing power, and halves the single-counterparty risk lenders price.
